title: The Laws of Thermodynamics

cards.h: Why you can't build a perpetual-motion machine
cards.b:
Inventors have long dreamed of a machine that runs forever, or that turns heat from the sea into free power for ships. Nature says no, and the laws that say it are among the most reliable in all of science.

Einstein once said thermodynamics is the one theory he was sure would never be overthrown, within its domain. The laws are short, but they limit every engine, fridge and power station on Earth.

cards.h: The zeroth law: temperature makes sense
cards.b:
If body A is in thermal equilibrium with C, and B is in equilibrium with C, then A and B are in equilibrium with each other. It sounds obvious, but it is what makes a thermometer meaningful: two things at the same reading will not exchange heat.

It was named 'zeroth' later, since it was seen as more basic than the first law, which was already numbered.

First law

change in internal energy = Q - W

Heat Q added to a system either raises its internal energy or is turned into work W done by the system. Energy is never created or destroyed.

Compress a bicycle pump quickly and the air gets hot: work done on the gas raises its energy. Julius Mayer and James Joule established this idea in the 1840s, showing heat and work are the same kind of thing.

Heat flows by itself from hot to cold, never the reverse. A cup of tea cools; it never spontaneously heats up by draining warmth from the room.

Two classic statements: Clausius (1850): no process can have the sole result of moving heat from cold to hot. Kelvin-Planck: no engine can turn heat entirely into work with nothing wasted. Some heat must always be rejected to a cold reservoir.

A heat engine takes heat Qh from a hot source, does work W, and throws out heat Qc to a cold sink. Efficiency = W / Qh.

Sadi Carnot (1824) showed that the best possible engine between temperatures Th and Tc (in kelvin) has:

Carnot efficiency

efficiency = 1 - Tc / Th

The hotter the source and the colder the sink, the better. No real engine can beat this.

A fridge is an engine running backwards: it uses work to pump heat from cold inside to warm outside. The back of your fridge is warm for this reason. An air-conditioner does the same.

The third law says you can never reach absolute zero, 0 K, in a finite number of steps. Scientists have reached billionths of a kelvin above it, but never zero itself.

An engine runs between 500 K and 300 K. Maximum efficiency = 1 - 300/500 = 1 - 0.6 = 0.4, or 40 percent.

If it takes in Qh = 1000 J, the most work it can give is W = 400 J, and it must reject Qc = 600 J (see the diagram).

A real engine does worse, perhaps 25 to 30 percent, because of friction and heat leaks. Check with the first law: Qh = W + Qc, so 1000 = 400 + 600.

• 'A fridge with the door open cools the room.' It heats it. The fridge pumps heat out of the box but also adds its motor's energy, so the room warms.
  • '100 percent efficient engines just need better design.' The second law forbids it, even in theory.
  • 'The first law means I cannot run out of useful energy.' Total energy is conserved, but useful energy is not: it degrades into spread-out heat.

Most of India's electricity still comes from coal-fired thermal plants, which are heat engines: coal heats steam, steam spins a turbine. Their efficiency is typically around one-third to 40 percent, close to what Carnot's law allows for their temperatures. The rest leaves as heat in cooling towers and chimneys.

India's rapid growth in air-conditioning, which moves heat out of homes, is a major source of rising power demand. Efficient (higher star-rated) units do the same cooling with less work.

• Zeroth: equal temperature means thermal equilibrium; this defines thermometers.
  • First: energy is conserved, change in U = Q - W.
  • Second: heat flows hot to cold; no engine is 100 percent efficient.
  • Carnot efficiency = 1 - Tc/Th (in kelvin).
  • Third: absolute zero cannot be reached.

Think about it

1. Why does raising the steam temperature in a power plant improve efficiency?
2. Why can't you cool your kitchen by leaving the fridge door open?
